---
title: "Excel Supplement, Chapter 15: Existing Data"
---

Chapter 15 says that the first task with a dataset somebody else made is not analysis but working out what the file can support. This supplement is that task, done as a checklist, on the corpus this book uses throughout.

It takes about twenty minutes. Run it on every dataset you did not collect yourself, before you write a single research question against it. Two of the things it finds here change how earlier chapters should be read, and neither of them is a defect in the data.

## Import, and the first thing to record

Import through **Data**, **From Text/CSV**, **65001: Unicode (UTF-8)**, with the **message** column set to **Text**. Chapter 24's supplement explains what happens otherwise, and the consequence is the first entry in your audit: **the file you analyzed is not the file you downloaded unless you controlled the import.**

Open a sheet called `provenance` and fill it in now, while you still know the answers:

| Field | For this corpus |
|---|---|
| source | `twitch_chat_sample` from the `v2v` package |
| obtained on | the date you downloaded it |
| version | the package version |
| original collection | Twitch IRC capture, November 2018 |
| documented sampling | 8 named anchor channels plus 42 stratified random, seed recorded |
| known transformations | IRC `#` prefix stripped from channel names |
| license or terms | as stated by the package |

The field people skip is **obtained on**, and it is the one that matters when the data is revised and your numbers no longer reproduce.

## The audit

Each is one formula, and each answers a question you would otherwise be assuming.

**How many rows, really?**

```
=COUNTA($A$2:$A$157081)
```

**157,080**, which matches the documentation.

**Are the identifiers unique?** The tempting formula is a classic:

```
=SUMPRODUCT(1/COUNTIF($A$2:$A$157081,$A$2:$A$157081))
```

**Do not run it on this file.** It counts distinct values by giving each row a weight of one over the number of times its value appears, which means Excel compares every row against every other row. At the 35,000 rows this fixture used to hold that was slow. At 157,080 it is about twenty-five billion comparisons, and Excel will appear to hang.

This is worth meeting once, because it is the shape of a problem you will hit again: **a formula whose cost grows with the square of the rows is fine on a sample and impossible on a corpus.** The fix is not a faster machine, it is a different method.

Copy column A, **Paste Special, Values** into a spare column, **Remove Duplicates**, and count what is left:

```
=COUNTA($M$2:$M$157081)
```

**157,080**, the same as the row count, so no duplicates. That runs instantly because Remove Duplicates sorts once rather than comparing every pair.

**Any empty values?**

```
=COUNTBLANK($D$2:$D$157081)
```

**2**, and both halves of that number are a surprise worth having.

There are no empty messages in this file. Not one. But Excel reports two blank cells, and it is right: **two messages in the corpus consist of a single apostrophe.** Excel treats a leading apostrophe as a marker meaning "store what follows as text", so it swallows the character and stores nothing. Two real messages disappear, silently, on import.

Nothing warns you, the cells look empty because they are empty, and `COUNTBLANK` will tell you your data has missing values when what it has is a character Excel refuses to keep. If a blank count ever disagrees with the file you imported, look at the raw text before believing the spreadsheet.

Then the sentinels. R writes a missing value into a CSV as the bare characters `NA`, so it is worth counting them:

```
=COUNTIF($D$2:$D$157081,"NA")
```

which returns **8**. That number is also not what it looks like. Chapter 19's supplement explains why `COUNTIF` is case-insensitive; here that means the count includes every message reading `na` as well as every one reading `NA`. The file holds **5** of the first and **3** of the second, and all eight are real messages that somebody typed. In this corpus `NA` is not a missing-value marker at all: it is how people write North America.

To count only the exact, case-sensitive string, use the tool Chapter 19 reached for:

```
=SUMPRODUCT(--EXACT($D$2:$D$157081,"NA"))
```

which returns **5**. Neither number is a missing value. **Before treating a sentinel as missing data, check whether it is a word in the language your participants are speaking.**

Do both counts for every column. A column that is 30 percent missing is a column you cannot use as you planned, and it is better to learn that now than after building an analysis on it.

**How many channels?** Copy the channel column, **Paste Special, Values**, **Remove Duplicates**: **228**, as documented.

**Are the documented anchor channels actually there?** One `COUNTIF` each, against the eight names the documentation lists:

```
=COUNTIF($B$2:$B$157081,"bobross")
```

All eight are present. **All eight return exactly 1,000**, which is the first hint of something the documentation does not mention.

**What is the real time span?** Convert the timestamps as Chapter 24's supplement does, then:

```
=MIN($H$2:$H$157081)   =MAX($H$2:$H$157081)
```

**2018-11-18 21:55** to **2018-11-24 18:20**: five days and twenty hours. Not "November 2018", which is what you would have written in your methods section from the documentation alone. A six-day window is a very different object from a month, and it constrains what you can say about anything that varies weekly.

## Where the documentation is wrong

The package help page says messages run **up to 509 characters**.

```
=MAX($G$2:$G$157081)
```

returns **500**. And:

```
=COUNTIF($G$2:$G$157081,">500")
```

returns **0**, and so does the same formula at `>509`.

Nine characters is nothing, and the reason for the gap is worth a great deal. The 509 is the longest message in the **full 21.9-million-message population** this sample was drawn from. It is correct about that population and it is printed in the help page for your 157,080-row extract.

**A documented figure can be true of the population and false of your file**, and nothing in the help page marks which it means. That is not a typo you can correct once; it is a question to ask of every number in a data dictionary.

## Where the documentation is right, and still not enough

This is the check that repays the twenty minutes.

Build the per-channel counts. Take your 228-row channel list and put beside it:

```
=COUNTIF($B$2:$B$157081,$J2)
```

Then look at the distribution rather than the individual numbers:

| Check | Formula | Result |
|---|---|---|
| channels at exactly 1,000 | `=COUNTIF($K$2:$K$229,1000)` | 137 |
| channels above 1,000 | `=COUNTIF($K$2:$K$229,">1000")` | 0 |
| channels below 100 | `=COUNTIF($K$2:$K$229,"<100")` | 41 |
| smallest channel | `=MIN($K$2:$K$229)` | 1 |

**One hundred and thirty-seven of 228 channels sit on exactly 1,000, and nothing is above it.**

Real counts do not do that. A hard ceiling with 137 channels resting on it and none above is a cap, applied when the sample was drawn.

The help page says so: *each channel contributes up to 1,000 messages to the sample*. So this check confirms the documentation rather than contradicting it, which is the outcome you should expect most of the time and should still run the check to establish.

Two lessons survive the confirmation. **That sentence is in the details section, below the column definitions**, and a reader who opens the help page to find out what the columns mean will never reach it. And the sentence says what was done without saying what it implies, which is that the corpus is balanced across channels rather than proportional to chat volume. Chapter 15 works through what that costs.

Sort the channel counts descending and look at the column, or chart them as a bar chart. The flat plateau followed by a cliff is visible instantly, and it is the reason this check is "look at the distribution" rather than "compute a statistic". **A summary statistic of the channel sizes would have hidden it completely**: the mean is unremarkable and the standard deviation tells you nothing about a ceiling.

## What to do with what you found

Write both findings into your limitations, and then work out what they change.

The cap means the corpus is balanced across channels rather than proportional to chat volume. Chapter 15 works through the consequence for Chapter 23's inequality figures and Chapter 25's group sizes. The short version: any quantity computed across channels is partly describing the sampling design.

Then make the check repeatable. Put the whole audit on one sheet with the formulas live, so that when the package updates, or when you get a fresh extract, you re-run it by replacing the data rather than by remembering what you checked. Chapter 24's supplement asks for a `decisions` sheet for the same reason, and the two belong in the same workbook.

## The checks worth running on any dataset

Generalized from the above, for a file you did not make:

1. Row count against the documentation.
2. Distinct count of the identifier, against the row count.
3. Blank count for every column.
4. Distinct count for every categorical column, and eyeball the list for case variants and near-duplicates. Chapter 24's supplement found `Minecraft` and `minecraft` in this very corpus.
5. Minimum and maximum for every numeric and date column, against what the documentation claims and against what is possible.
6. The distribution of records per group, looking for round numbers, ceilings and floors.
7. Every documented property that can be expressed as a formula, actually expressed as one.

Number seven is the whole method. **Documentation is a claim about the data, and a claim you can check in a spreadsheet is a claim you should check in a spreadsheet.**

## What Excel will not do for you

It will not tell you whether the 42 non-anchor channels really were drawn as documented, or what was in the 1.6 GB dump that did not make it into these 157,080 rows. Those questions go to whoever made the file, and "we asked and could not find out" is a legitimate and reportable answer.

It will also not tell you whether the data fits your question, which is the judgment this whole chapter is about. What it does is make sure that when you make that judgment, you are making it about the file you actually have rather than the one the documentation describes.
